So fear Allah and seek provision in a good manner."

His saying: ﴿and the good tidings came to him﴾. It has been said that the good tidings were of Isaac and Jacob. It has also been said that they were of the destruction of the people of Lot.

His saying: ﴿he began to argue with Us﴾. Its meaning: Abraham began to argue with Us. The arguing here is like what He said in the surahs of al-Dhariyat and al-Hijr: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾. If it is said: How is it permissible for Abraham to argue with his Lord concerning a matter that He had decreed and commanded?

The answer: This arguing was with the angels, not with the Lord, and He said "with Us" in a broad (tawassu') use of speech. In the exegesis it is related that his arguing was that he said to the angels: "Do you see that if there were fifty believers in the cities of the people of Lot, would you destroy them?" They said: "No." He said: "Do you see that if there were forty among them, would you destroy them?" They said: "No." He kept decreasing by tens until it reached five persons, and Abraham had thought that the wife of Lot was a believer, and she was the fifth, and he did not know that she was a disbeliever. So the number of believers did not reach five ﴿among the people of Lot﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 75:

And the saying of Allah Most High, ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, plaintive, and turning back (to Allah) in repentance﴾, has already been explained earlier. It is related from Bakr ibn Abdullah al-Muzani that he said: "The one who turns back (munib) is the one whose heart is with Allah Most High." The true meaning of inabah (turning back in repentance) is return (ruju'). It is said: nāba, āba and anāba, when he returned.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 76:

The words of the Most High, ﴿O Ibrahim, turn away from this﴾. The meaning of the verse: the angels said, "O Ibrahim, turn away from disputing."

His words, ﴿Indeed, the command of your Lord has come﴾, meaning: the decree of your Lord and the judgment of your Lord. And His words, {And indeed, there will come to them a punishment that cannot be turned back}, meaning: not diverted away from them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 77:

His saying: ﴿When Our messengers came to Lut﴾. These messengers were the ones who had been with Ibrahim. They came to Lut in the form of beardless young men, handsome of face, clean of clothing, and fragrant [in their scent].

In the narrative: they met Lut while he was gathering firewood, and they asked him for hospitality. He carried the firewood and the angels followed him. He passed by a group of his people with them, and they winked at one another. Lut said to them: "Indeed my people are the worst of God's creation." Then he passed by another group of them with them, and they also winked at one another. Lut said a second time: "Indeed my people are the worst of God's creation, may God Most High." Then he passed by yet another group of them with them, and they winked at one another again. Lut said a third time: "Indeed my people are the worst of God's creation." God Most High had said to Jibril: "Do not destroy them until Lut has testified against them three times." So whenever Lut said this statement, Jibril said to the angels who were with him: "Bear witness."

As for His saying: ﴿He was distressed on their account﴾, its meaning is: their coming grieved him. And His saying: ﴿and his heart constricted for them﴾: it is said "ḍāqa dharʿan (bi-kadhā)" ("so-and-so's ḍharʿ was constricted by such-and-such") when a person falls into something disagreeable from which he cannot bear to escape. (Ḍharʿ, literally "forearm," figuratively the capacity to bear something.)

The meaning of the verse here is: he was constricted in his capacity to protect them and to prevent their people from speaking [of them].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he said, "This is a distressing day."﴾ ʿAṣīb means: severe. The poet said:

(Indeed, if you are not content with Bakr ibn Wa'il, there will come for you a severe day in Iraq.)

That is: severe. And another said:

(A day of ʿaṣīb that binds the heroes, binding the tall spears' strength.)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And his people came hastening toward him﴾ — the verse. "Yuhra'una ilayh" (they hasten toward him) means: they rush and run. We have already explained that Lut had passed by them with them.

In another narration: the angels came to the house of Lut, peace be upon him, and Lut was in his house. His wicked, disbelieving wife went to his people and informed them of the arrival of these men. When they heard, they came seeking the abomination.

His saying: ﴿And before this they had been doing evil deeds﴾ means: the abominations, which are: coming to men.

His saying: ﴿He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you"﴾ — concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: he offered them his own daughters in marriage and wedlock. If someone says: how is it permissible for a polytheist to marry a Muslim woman?

The answer: that was permissible in their law. Some said: he offered them on the condition of Islam.

The second opinion — and it is the view of Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others — is that he offered them their women, and called them his daughters, because the Prophet is to the community like a father. In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them." Some said: he said this by way of deflection, not as a firm statement, and they did not accept this view, because he was protected from lying. His saying: ﴿they are purer for you﴾ means: they are lawful for you.

His saying: ﴿So fear Allah and do not disgrace me regarding my guests﴾ means: fear Allah and do not shame me in front of my guests. ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?﴾ means: Is there not among you a man who enjoins the good and repels the people from my guests? It is narrated from Ikrimah that he said: the meaning of His saying ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?﴾ is: Is there not among you a man who says, "There is no god but Allah"?

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 79:

His words: ﴿They said: "You know well that we have no right to your daughters; indeed you know what we want."﴾ In this there are two meanings. The first: "We have no right to your daughters," that is, no need and no desire. The second: "We have no right to your daughters," that is, no marriage. His words ﴿And indeed you know what we desire﴾ mean: we desire the posteriors of men.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 80:

The words of the Most High: ﴿He said, "If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a strong support."﴾ Al-quwwa (power) here is either physical strength in the body, or strength through followers. Al-rukn al-shadid (the strong support) is protection through one's clan.

It has been established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Lut; he used to take refuge in a strong support." That is, in Allah. Narrated by Abu Hurayra.

And from Abu Hurayra, he said: "Allah did not send any prophet after that except with protection from his people."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 81:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O Lut, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you."﴾ It is related that they came and broke open the door of Lut and intended to enter. In another narration: they were contending with Lut at the door, so Jibril said, "O Lut, open the door and let them enter." When they entered, he struck their faces with his wing, and they were all blinded. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they had sought to seduce him from his guests, so We obliterated their eyes.﴾ Then they said, "O Lut, you have brought us a people of sorcerers; you will see what you will meet from us tomorrow," and they had come in the evening.

His saying: ﴿They will never reach you﴾ has a known meaning.

His saying: ﴿So travel with your family in a part of the night﴾ was read as "fasir" from al-sara (the journey by night), and "fa-asri" from al-isra' (the night journey). Al-sara is travel by night. A poet said:

(At dawn the people praise the night journey, and the veils of sleep clear away from me.)

His saying: ﴿asri﴾ is from al-isra', and the two meanings are one. His saying: ﴿in a part of the night﴾ means: at the last part of the night. It was also said that it means the first watch of the night. A poet said:

(And a wailing woman wails in a part of the night, over a dead man at the edge of the highland.)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let none of you turn around, except your wife﴾ is read with the nominative "imra'atuka" and also with the accusative "imra'ataka." The accusative reading means: travel with your family except your wife. The nominative reading means: let none of you turn around, except your wife; for she will turn around. It is related that when she heard the noise of the destruction of the people, she turned back, and a stone struck her and she died. God had commanded Lut and his family not to turn around.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, what will befall them will befall her﴾ is clear in meaning. His saying: ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾: it is related that when Lut, peace be upon him, heard this from Jibril, he said, "O Jibril, I want them to be destroyed now." So he replied to him, answering: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾

The Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on Surah 11, verse 82:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿When Our command came﴾ means: Our punishment. And His words: ﴿We made its highest part its lowest﴾ It is related that Jibril placed his wing beneath the cities of Lut, and they were five cities, and in them were four hundred thousand (people). It was also said: in them were four million. Then he lifted the cities until they came close to the sky, and the inhabitants of the sky heard the crowing of roosters and the barking of dogs. It is related that no vessel was overturned for them and no sleeper was awakened for them. Then he overturned them, and Allah, exalted is He, sent stones after them. This is the meaning of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon it stones of sijjil [baked clay]﴾.

And His words: ﴿of sijjil﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: sang and gil (stone and clay). The word sijjil is Persian, arabicized (mu'arrab).

It was also said: it was clay baked like brick.

The second opinion: sijjil is the lowest heaven.

The third opinion: sijjil is sijjin, with the nun replaced by a lam. It was also said: sijjil is derived from sajl, which is the bucket's rope. The poet said:

(I am the green one; whoever knows me knows / green of skin, from a house of the Arabs)
(Whoever competes with me in drawing water competes with a generous man / who fills the bucket up to the rope's knot)

The meaning of sijjil in the verse is sending (al-irsal), that is, the sending of stones.

And His words: ﴿arranged in layers [mandud]﴾ mean: one following another.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 83:

And His saying: ﴿marked﴾, that is: distinguished (mu'allamah). It is related in the narration that there were red streaks upon them against a black background.

The second opinion: "marked" means that upon them were the names of the people (for whom they were destined). It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that upon them was something resembling seal-rings.

His saying: ﴿with your Lord﴾ — its meaning is apparent.

And His saying: ﴿and it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾ means: it is not far from the wrongdoers of Makkah.

It has been related in some reports that upon the head of every wrongdoer there is a stone suspended in the sky, awaiting the command of God Most High. This is among the strange reports, and God knows best.

In some accounts: there was among them a man in the Haram, and the stone remained suspended in the sky for forty days until the man came out [and the stone struck him]. It is also related that the stone followed their fugitives and travelers wherever they were in the lands, until they perished.

And some of them mentioned that God Most High destroyed the cities of Lut except Za'ar, for He left it for Lut and his family.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 84:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And to Madyan We sent their brother Shu'ayb﴾. We have already explained that the brotherhood here is brotherhood by lineage, not brotherhood in religion. Some of them said: there was also no brotherhood of lineage between Shu'ayb and the people of Madyan, and he was a stranger among them; he meant by "brotherhood" only kinship in humanity (al-mujanasah fi al-bashariyyah). The sound view is the first.

And His saying: ﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾ — its meaning is clear. His saying: ﴿And do not diminish the measure and the scale﴾ means: and do not cheat in the measure and the scale (la tabkhasu, i.e. do not defraud). They, despite their polytheism, used to cheat in measure and weight.

It is related from Abdullah ibn Umar that when he passed by the market he would say: "O merchants, give full measure and give full weight, for you have heard what Allah did to the people of Shu'ayb."

And from Ibn Abbas there is something close to this.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾. Mujahid said: that is, in abundance and ample means.

His saying: ﴿And indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾ — that is, encompassing you so that it destroys you.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 85:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight with justice﴾ — that is, with fairness (al-'adl).

It is also said: [it means] straightening the tongue of the balance (taqwim lisan al-mizan). As for His words: ﴿And do not diminish for the people their things﴾ — that is, do not reduce the people's goods. And His words: ﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 86:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What remains with Allah is better for you, if you are believers﴾. Its meaning: what Allah has left for you of the lawful (ḥalāl) is better than what you take by defrauding in the measure and the scale. It has also been said: "What remains with Allah" means the obedience (ṭāʿa) of Allah. His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾, i.e., if you are believers that what you have of the provision (rizq) of Allah, exalted is He, and His bounty (ʿaṭāʾ) is [better].

His saying: ﴿And I am not a watcher over you﴾. It has been said its meaning is: I have not been commanded to fight you. It has also been said: "I am not a watcher over you" means: I am not a guardian (wakīl).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 87:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we not do with our wealth what we wish?"﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: "Does your religion command you (to do this)?" The second: "Does your Qur'an (recitation) command you that we abandon..." [Here "Qur'an" is read in the sense of recitation/scripture, as the commentator presents it.] ﴿what our fathers worshipped, or that we not do with our wealth what we wish﴾, meaning: by way of deficiency and excess (in measure and weight). It was also said: by clipping (debasing) the dirhams and dinars. He had forbidden them from that and claimed that it was unlawful for them.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾ concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: "Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided, according to your own claim." They said this mockingly.

The second: its meaning is: "Indeed, you are the foolish, the witless."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 88:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Said he: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord"﴾. Its meaning: upon clear explanation (bayan) from my Lord.

And His saying: ﴿and He has provided me from Him with goodly provision﴾. Its meaning: lawful provision (rizqan halalan). And in the narrative: that Shu'ayb was a man of much wealth. It has also been said: the goodly provision here is prophethood (al-nubuwwah).

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in that which I forbid you from﴾. Its meaning: I do not intend to command you to something and then act contrary to it.

And His saying: ﴿I intend nothing but reform, as much as I am able﴾. Its meaning is apparent.

And His saying: ﴿And my success is not but through Allah﴾. This is evidence that obedience is not brought about except by the success (tawfiq) of Allah, and tawfiq from Allah is facilitation, ease, and assistance.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾. That is: upon Him I have depended (i'timad).

And His saying: ﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾. Its meaning: to Him I return.

And O my people, let not my opposition (shiqaq) bring upon you the like of what befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih. Here the verb "yajrimannakum" means: let it not earn you, nor lead you (to), my opposition, i.e., my disagreement with you over a course of action, such that it strikes you. So it will strike you: the like of what struck the people of Noah, [namely] by drowning; or the people of Hud, [namely] by the wind; or the people of Salih, [namely] by the Blast, the thunderous cry.

And His saying: "And the people of Lut are not far from you" (﴿وَمَا قوم لوط مِنْكُم بِبَعِيد﴾). It is said: they were neighbours of the people of Lut in their dwellings, and their cities were close to one another.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 90:

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And ask forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾. The meaning has already been explained. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving﴾, there are two meanings concerning al-Wadud (the Loving):

The first: al-Wadud is the one who loves His servants.

The second: or al-Wadud is in the sense of al-mawdud (the one who is loved), i.e., the servants love Him for His bounty and His kindness.

And in the well-known report, the Prophet said: "Love Allah for the blessings He nourishes you with, love me with the love of Allah, and love the people of my household for my love."

And in some reports from the Prophet, he said: "Shu'ayb was the orator of the prophets."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 91:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say"﴾. Its meaning: we do not understand much of what you say.

And His saying: ﴿And indeed, we see you as weak among us﴾. Concerning "weak" (ḍaʿīf) there are several views. The majority of the exegetes hold that "weak" here means blind in sight (ḍarīr bi-l-baṣar). It is said that this is the dialect of Himyar.

The second view: "weak" means weak in body.

The third: that he had few followers.

And His saying: ﴿Had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾, i.e., had it not been for your kin, we would have stoned you. Stoning (al-rajm) is the most hideous of killings. And His saying: ﴿And you are not esteemed by us﴾, meaning: you are not honoured (ʿazīz) among us, and we only leave you alone because of the standing of your clan.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 92:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "O my people, is my kinsfolk more powerful against you than Allah?"﴾ Its meaning: Is my kinsfolk more awe-inspiring and more protective to you than Allah, may He be exalted? The real meaning is: You have refrained from killing me out of regard for my kinsfolk, so it is more fitting that you should protect me for the sake of Allah, may He be exalted.

And His saying: ﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs, cast away.﴾ Its meaning: You have thrown the command of Allah, may He be exalted, behind your backs. It is said: "So-and-so made such-and-such a thing behind his back (zihriyyan)," meaning: he threw it behind his back.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do.﴾ Its apparent meaning is clear.

Al-Azhari (al-Azhari, the lexicographer) mentioned, regarding the estimation and meaning of the verse, saying: "You claim that you refrain from killing me out of honour for my kinsfolk, so it is more fitting that you honour the command of Allah and follow it." The real meaning is a rebuke of the one who fears people and does not fear Allah. He said: And His saying: ﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs, cast away.﴾ The Arabs say: "So-and-so made such-and-such a thing a matter of neglect (bi-zahr) when he left it and paid it no attention." The poet said:

(Tamim ibn Qays, let not my need be left in neglect... so that it does not weary him to answer it)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 93:

The Exalted One's saying: ﴿And O my people, act according to your position﴾. It is said: al-makanah (position) is the condition in which a person is able to carry out the action.

The meaning of the verse: act according to your capacity and your station, ﴿indeed I am acting﴾ according to my capacity and my station, ﴿so you will come to know﴾ who will be saved and who will perish.

The verse contains a threat and a severe warning, and in the Qur'an the phrase ﴿so you will come to know﴾ appears only in this verse.

As for the Exalted One's saying: ﴿upon whom will come a punishment that will disgrace him﴾, i.e., humiliate him and expose him, ﴿and who is a liar﴾: there is an ellipsis in it, and the implied sense of the verse is: you will come to know upon whom will come a punishment that disgraces him, and who is a liar, he too will be disgraced.

As for His saying: ﴿And wait; indeed I am with you, a waiter﴾, it means: wait, indeed I am waiting along with you.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 94:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Our command came⦆ means: when the time of Our punishment came, ﴿We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and the ones who did wrong were seized by the Sayha (al-sayha, the cry)﴾. The sayha means destruction. The Arabs say: "So-and-so cried out (sāha) against so-and-so's property," meaning: he destroyed it. Imru' al-Qays said:

(Leave aside the plunder that was cried out upon in its tents... but tell a tale of what the riding camels bore)

It is related that ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) quoted this line in some of his affairs.

It is also said that the sayha here is the cry of Jibril (peace be upon him), who cried out at them with a single cry, and they all died to the last of them. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So they became, in their homes, prostrate corpses﴾, meaning: dead and lifeless, not moving.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 95:

His saying: ﴿As if they had never dwelt therein﴾ means: as if they had never been living there in comfort and joy.

And His saying: ﴿Away with Madyan, just as Thamud were done away with﴾ means: Away with (destruction for) Madyan, just as Thamud were ruined and destroyed.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 96:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority﴾. Its meaning: with Our nine signs. "A clear authority" means a manifest proof. Every instance of "sultan" (authority) mentioned in the Qur'an carries the meaning of proof. It has also been said: sultan is derived from al-saliṭ (olive oil), which is the oil by which one is illuminated.

al-Samʿani said: His saying, ﴿to Pharaoh and his establishment﴾: "and his establishment (al-mala')" is well known. His saying, ﴿but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not right conduct﴾: its meaning is, they followed Pharaoh's command in taking himself as a god and in abandoning faith in Moses. ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not right conduct﴾ means: it did not guide to good and righteousness.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 98:

The words of the Most High: ﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection﴾ mean: he will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And will bring them to the Fire﴾ means: he will cause them to enter the Fire. ﴿And wretched is the watering place to which they are brought﴾ means: wretched is the one who enters, and wretched is the place of entering.

And in some of the musnads: from Abu Burdah, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will gather the creation in one level plain. Then for every people will be raised up the deities they used to worship besides Allah, and they will lead them to the Fire. The believers will remain, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say to them: 'What are you waiting for?' They will say: 'We are waiting for a Lord whom we used to worship in the unseen.' He will say to them: 'Do you know Him?' They will say: 'If He wills, He will make us know Himself.' He said: 'Then He will manifest Himself to them, and they will fall down prostrate before Him. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, will say: O people of monotheism, raise your heads, for I have made Paradise obligatory for you, and I have made in place of each one of you a Jew or a Christian.'"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 99:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse﴾ means: in this world a curse by the punishment of separation (al-tafriq), ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection﴾ a curse by the punishment of the Fire. And His saying: ﴿Wretched is the gift that is given﴾ means: wretched is the curse after the curse. Abu 'Ubayda said: that is, wretched is the aid (al-mu'an), and its meaning here is that the curse was made for them in the place of aid. It was also said: wretched is the giving of the one who gives.

This is the commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on Surah 11, verse 100.

His words, may God Most High have mercy on him, on the saying of God Most High: ﴿That is among the news of the towns which We relate to you.﴾ Its meaning: from the reports of the towns We relate to you. ﴿Of them some are standing and some are reaped.﴾ That is: of them some are inhabited and some are ruined. It was also said that its meaning is: "Of them some are standing," that is, the walls remain while the roofs have fallen; and "of them some are reaped," that is, their traces have been effaced.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 101:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾. He has already explained this before. And His words: ﴿So their gods, whom they invoked besides Allah, did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came﴾ means: by the punishment. And His words: ﴿and they added nothing to them but ruin﴾, i.e., nothing but loss (takhsir). It was also said: nothing but destruction (tadmir).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 102:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are wrongdoing﴾. The aspect of the comparison is that His seizing of these (people) in a state of wrongdoing and polytheism is like His seizing of the people of the cities when they were in a similar state of wrongdoing and polytheism. And His saying: ﴿Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe﴾ — its meaning is apparent.

It has been firmly established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, Allah gives respite to the wrongdoer — or gives him rope — until, when He seizes him, He does not let him go." Then he recited the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are wrongdoing﴾. The report is in the "Two Sahihs" (al-Sahihayn), narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 103:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ means: a lesson (ʿibrah) ﴿for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter﴾. The apparent meaning is clear. ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered﴾, meaning: the Day of Resurrection, on which Allah will gather the first and the last. ﴿And that is a Day witnessed﴾, meaning: all creation will witness it. It has also been said: the people of the heavens and the people of the earth.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 104:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And We do not delay it except for a term already counted.﴾ That is: except until a time known with Allah, not with the people.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: The lifespan of this world is seven thousand years; none of you knows how much of it has passed and how much remains.

And His saying: ﴿On the Day it comes﴾. It is also read as "yawma ya'ti" with a ya' (يَوْم يَأْتِي). Al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) and Sibawayh reported that the Arabs say "لَا أدر" (lā adr), meaning "لَا أَدْرِي" (lā adrī, "I do not know"), dropping the final long vowel. Al-Farra' mentioned that the Arabs make do with the kasra (short vowel) in place of the ya' that follows it.

And His saying: ﴿No soul will speak except by His permission﴾. There is a well-known question regarding this verse: Allah the Exalted has said elsewhere: ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other﴾, yet here He says: ﴿No soul will speak except by His permission﴾. So how can the two be reconciled?

The answer: We have mentioned that there are stations on the Day of Resurrection. In one station they speak and question one another; in another station they are silent and do not speak; and in another station their mouths are sealed and their limbs speak. It has been said other than this, and we have explained it.

And His saying: ﴿So among them are the wretched and the blessed﴾. Wretchedness (al-shaqawah) is the strength of the causes of affliction, and blessedness (al-sa'adah) is the strength of the causes of bounty. The meaning of the verse here, according to Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, the orthodox majority), is: among them is one who has been predestined to wretchedness, and among them is one who has been predestined to blessedness.

In the authentic reports with chains of narration: when 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf was on his deathbed, he fell unconscious. When he regained consciousness, he said: "Two angels came to me, harsh and rough, dragged me, and said: 'Come, let us bring you before the Mighty, the Trustworthy.'" He said: "Then an angel met them and said: 'Where are you taking him?' They said: 'We are bringing him before the Mighty, the Trustworthy.' He said to them: 'Let him go, for he is among those whose blessedness was decreed in the first Remembrance (al-dhikr al-awwal).'"

It is also established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the report about the angel of the wombs: "When He has written his term, his deeds, and his provision, it says: 'O Lord, is he wretched or blessed?' Then Allah the Exalted decides, and the angel writes." Muslim transmitted it.

Ibn 'Umar reported from 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) that when the words of the Exalted were revealed, ﴿So among them are the wretched and the blessed﴾, 'Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, for what purpose is action? Are we to act in a matter that has already been concluded, and the pens have already run with it, or in a matter that has not yet been concluded?" He said: "Rather, in a matter that has already been concluded and the pens have already run with it, O 'Umar. But each is made easy for that for which he was created." Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) cited it in his Jami'.

Some have said: the blessedness and wretchedness here refer to provision and deprivation. Others have said: wretchedness is by evil deeds, and blessedness is by good deeds. The transmitted and authentic position is the first.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 106:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them there will be groaning and wailing﴾. This verse is counted among the difficult passages of the Qur'an, and the scholars have offered many opinions concerning it. We mention what is relied upon:

As for al-zafir (groaning): it is said to be a sound in the throat, and al-shahiq (wailing) is a sound in the chest. It is also said that al-zafir is the first braying of donkeys, and al-shahiq is the last braying of donkeys.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 107:

As for His saying: ﴿abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, according to the transmitted meaning: al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning a group of believers whom God, exalted is He, will cause to enter the Fire and then bring them out of it into Paradise, and they are called the Jahannamiyyun (the people of Hell). It is also established through the narration of Jabir that the Prophet said: "God will bring out from the Fire a people who have become charred (ḥumam), and He will admit them into Paradise."

There are many reports on this subject.

According to this view, the meaning of the verse is: as for those who were wretched, these are the ones whom He causes to enter the Fire, ﴿for them therein is groaning and wailing﴾. The apparent meaning of ﴿abiding therein﴾ is remaining in it ﴿for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾; this is an expression for a long duration of stay.

As for His saying: ﴿except as your Lord wills; indeed your Lord is the doer of what He intends﴾, the exception applies to what comes after their being brought out of the Fire through the intercession of the Prophets and the believers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 108:

As for his saying, ﴿And as for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden﴾, he meant by it the believers whom He admitted into the Garden without their entering the Fire. His saying, ﴿abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, means: remaining therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure. He used this as a metaphor for a long duration of stay. The Arabs say something similar and mean by it eternity: they say, "I will not come to you as long as the heavens and the earth endure," meaning, "I will never come to you," and "I will not come to you as long as there is a drop of water in the sea," meaning, "I will never come to you." Thus this statement follows the manner of Arabic speech. His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, the exception applies to the period they spent in the Fire before being admitted into the Garden.

There are two other well-known opinions regarding the verse, besides this one, among the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani):

The first: the meaning of His saying, ﴿abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ is according to its apparent sense, that is, the duration of the existence of the heavens and the earth. His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, means: other than what your Lord wills of an addition to the duration of their existence. al-Farra' relates from the Arabs that they say, "You owe me a thousand, except the two thousands," meaning: other than the two thousands that preceded.

The second opinion: the meaning of His saying, ﴿abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ is: for as long as the heavens and earth of the Garden endure. His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, the exception pertains to the time of standing (for judgment) on the Day of Resurrection and the period of staying in the grave.

A third opinion regarding the exception has also been stated: that He said, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, meaning: had He willed, He would have cut off their eternal abiding, but He does not will it. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is not for us to return to it, unless God wills, the Lord of the worlds﴾, and "but He does not will it." And His saying, ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Accomplisher of what He intends﴾, means: nothing can prevent Him. And in the second verse He said, ﴿a gift not cut off﴾, meaning: not interrupted.

In some tafsir works it is related from Abu Hurayrah that he said: a time will come upon Hell when no one will remain in it. And from al-Hasan al-Basri something close to this.

The meaning of this, according to the people of the Sunnah, if it is established, is that what is intended is the place in the Fire where the believers are, and then they will leave it, so no one will remain in it. As for the places of the disbelievers, they will be filled with them forever and ever, as the Book and the Sunnah have declared. We seek refuge with God from the Fire.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 109:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So do not be in doubt about what these people worship﴾ — "in doubt" means in suspicion. ﴿What these people worship﴾ — it is said: the address is directed to him (the Prophet ﷺ), but what is meant is the community (ummah).

His words: ﴿They worship only as their fathers worshipped before.﴾ The meaning is apparent.

His words: ﴿And indeed, We will give them their share in full, without diminution.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said its meaning: We will give them their share of good and evil in full, without any reduction.

The Qur'anic verse "And We had certainly given Moses the Book, but it was disputed over" — the meaning of the verse is consolation for the Prophet. It is as if He said: if they dispute with you and do not believe in you, then they disputed with Moses too and did not believe in him.

His saying, ﴿And had it not been for a word that had already preceded from your Lord﴾, means: had it not been for what had preceded of God's decree to delay the punishment until the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, ﴿it would have been decided between them﴾, means: they would have been punished immediately and destroyed.

His saying, ﴿And indeed, they are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾, its meaning is apparent.

And as for "wa-in kullan" (and indeed, each): it has been read as "wa-in" and "wa-inna," both with light and with heavy pronunciation. As for "in" and "inna," they said: both have the same meaning. The poet said:

((And the face of) fine neck... as if his two breasts were two ivory cups (ḥuqqān)).

Its meaning: as if his two breasts were two ivory cups.

And His saying: ﴿lamā﴾ with light pronunciation. It has been said: "lamā" means "liman" (for whoever), and it is said: the lām is for oath, as if Allah the Exalted said: "And indeed each, by Allah, your Lord will surely pay them in full for their deeds." As for His saying "lamā" with heavy pronunciation: it has been said that the meaning of "lamā" with heavy pronunciation is the same as its meaning with light pronunciation. This was related by al-Māzinī.

Al-Azharī said: the most correct meaning is that "lamā" means "illā" (except/only), meaning: "and except that your Lord will surely pay them in full for their deeds. ﴿Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do.﴾" The meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 112:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remain upright as you have been commanded﴾. The meaning of istiqamah (steadfastness, uprightness) is perseverance in what the command and the prohibition require. It has been narrated from the Prophet, through the transmission of Abu Muslim al-Khawlani, from Umar ibn al-Khattab (but the sound report is from Abu Dharr), that he said: "Even if you prayed until you became like bent bows (al-hana, sing. hanya), and fasted until you became like dry palm-sprigs (al-hana'ir, sing. hanira), meaning: like stakes (al-awtad), and then two were dearer to you than one, you would not reach the limit of istiqamah." This report was related by a group of ascetics (zuhhad). Hatim al-Asamm related it from Shaqiq, from Ibrahim ibn Adham, from Malik ibn Dinar, from Abu Muslim, with this chain.

And in the well-known report: the Prophet said: "Be upright, and you will not be able to count [your deeds]; and none will maintain the wudu' except a believer." And from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Istiqamah is that you remain steadfast in the command and the prohibition, and do not swerve as foxes swerve. This is a well-known report.

Other things have been related about istiqamah besides this, which will be mentioned in its place.

And in the well-known report also: the Prophet said: "Hud has grayed me." In this there are two meanings:

One of them: he said this because of the abundance of what Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in this surah of the destruction of the past generations (qurun) and the bygone nations (umam).

The second meaning: he said it because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remain upright as you have been commanded﴾.

And His saying: ﴿And those who turned in repentance with you﴾ means: those who embraced Islam with you. And His saying: ﴿And do not transgress﴾ has two meanings: One of them: "And do not transgress in uprightness," meaning: do not add to what you have been commanded and forbidden, so that you forbid what Allah has made lawful and burden yourselves with what Allah has not prescribed and what the Messenger and his Companions did not do.

The second meaning: transgression (tughyan) is insolence (batar) due to the increase of blessing. It was also said: tughyan and baghy have the same meaning.

﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾: the meaning is apparent.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 113:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged, lest the Fire touch you.﴾ Al-rukun (inclination) is love, affection, and leaning of the heart. It is reported from Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi that he said: it is contentment with their deeds. It is reported from al-Suddi that he said: it is flattery toward them. It is reported from Ikrimah that he said: it is obeying them. His words ﴿lest the Fire touch you﴾ mean: lest the Fire afflict you.

His words ﴿And you have no protectors other than Allah, and then you would not be helped﴾ are clear in meaning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 114:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "The two ends of the day" are the dawn (Subh) and the afternoon ('Asr), ﴿and at the approaches of the night﴾ are the sunset (Maghrib) and the night prayer ('Isha').

Mujahid said: "The two ends of the day" are the dawn (Subh), the noon (Zuhr) and the afternoon ('Asr), and "at the approaches of the night" are the sunset (Maghrib) and the night prayer ('Isha').

According to this view, the verse encompasses the five obligatory prayers. It is also reported from some of them: "The two ends of the day" are the dawn and the sunset, and "at the approaches of the night" is the 'Atamah (the late night prayer, i.e. 'Isha').

The meaning of His saying ﴿zulafan min al-layl﴾ (at the approaches of the night) is the hours of the night. It was also said: an hour of the night. Mujahid recited "wa-zulfan min al-layl" (with a dhamma and the form zulfa), and Ibn Muhaysin recited "wa-zulafan min al-layl" (with a fatha). The well-known reading is "zulafan min al-layl." The poet said:

(The nights folded into approaches after approaches... until the crescent of the moon bent and curved)

The occasion of the revelation of the verse: it is what has been narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that "a man came to the Prophet and said: O Messenger of Allah, I entered an orchard and I came upon a woman, and I touched her as a man touches his wife, except that I did not have intercourse with her. Here I am before you, so do with me as you wish." So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse: ﴿And establish prayer﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾. Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: "O Messenger of Allah" – and in another narration he said: a man from the people came and said: "O Messenger of Allah" – "is this specific to him, or is it general for the Muslims?" The Messenger of Allah said: "Rather, it is general for the Muslims."

Abu Umamah al-Bahili narrated that "a man came to the Messenger of Allah and said: O Messenger of Allah, I have committed a prescribed offence, so enforce it upon me. He said: Did you not pray with us this prayer, and you had purified yourself? He said: Yes. He, peace be upon him, said: Go, for Allah has forgiven you what you committed."

'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, narrated that the Prophet said: "If there were a river at the door of one of you in which he bathed five times a day, would any of his filth remain?" They said: "No, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "That is the likeness of the five prayers, by which Allah erases sins." This is a sound report.

Regarding the expiation of sins by the five prayers, there is the report of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, in which it is mentioned: "Every prayer expiates what is between it and the next prayer." It is also reported from Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was sitting in the shade of a tree, took a dry branch from it and shook it, so its leaves fell. Then he said: "Do you know why I did this?" They said: "No." He said: "Whoever purifies himself and prays the five prayers, his sins fall away from him just as these leaves have fallen from this branch." And from Abu al-Yusr, a man of the Ansar, that "a woman came to him seeking to buy dates, and he said: In the shop there are dates better than what you see. She said: So she entered the shop, and he kissed her and embraced her, and he touched her as a man touches his wife, except that he did not have intercourse with her. Then he came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and mentioned that to him, and said: Do with me as you wish. The Prophet remained silent for a while, then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾."

It is also narrated from Mu'adh that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, advise me." He said: "Fear Allah wherever you are, follow a bad deed with a good deed and it will erase it, and deal with people with good character."

All these reports indicate the meaning of the verse.

In some tafsir works it is mentioned that a man sat with Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and Ibn al-Musayyib heard him say: "O Allah, make me successful in the enduring good deeds." Sa'id said to him: "And what are the enduring good deeds?" He said: "The five prayers." Sa'id said: "No. Rather, the enduring good deeds are: Glory be to Allah, Praise be to Allah, There is no god but Allah, Allah is the Greatest, and there is no power and no strength except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty. And the five prayers are (among) the good deeds."

His saying: ﴿That is a reminder for those who remember﴾ means: that is an admonition for those who take heed.

Almost the whole passage is the verse itself, quoted in full, so I translate it accordingly.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.﴾ The apparent meaning is an exhortation to patience upon these prayers, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 116:

His saying: ﴿Why were there not among the generations before you﴾ – the verse. His saying: "Fa-law" (why then / why not) means: "fa-hal" (then why not), and it is said: "fa-lam la" (why not). The verse is for reproach and wonder. His saying: ﴿those of residue﴾ – it is said: those of obedience. And it is said: those of discernment. And it is said: those of a remnant of good. It is said: "So-and-so is upon a remnant of good" when he is upon obedience, or a trace of intellect, or upon a praiseworthy quality. His saying: ﴿who forbid corruption in the earth﴾ – meaning: they stand up to forbid corruption. His saying: ﴿except a few﴾ – this is an exceptive clause of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), and its meaning: "but a few of those whom We saved from the generations [who] forbade corruption."

His saying: ﴿of those We saved from them. And those who did wrong followed what they were given in luxury therein﴾ – al-mutraf: he is the one who is given to comfort. It is said: he is the one accustomed to ease and pleasure. It is said: al-mutraf is the one whom wealth and blessing have made insolent.

So the meaning of the verse: "And those who did wrong followed what they had been accustomed to of indulging in desires and pleasures."

﴿And they were criminals﴾ – clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 117:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities unjustly while their people were reforming﴾. In this verse there are two opinions.

The first: He does not destroy them merely for associating partners with Him, so long as they practise fairness among themselves and one of them does not wrong another.

The second: It means that Allah does not wrong the people of a town by destroying them without any wrongdoing on their part. The first is the more well known.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 118:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾ mean: And had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind upon one religion.

And His words: ﴿but they will not cease to differ﴾ are intended to refer to: the people of falsehood, such as the Jews, the Christians, the Magians, and the people of polytheism; and likewise whoever opposes the Sunnah among the people of the qibla.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 119:

And His saying: ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy﴾, meaning: but those on whom your Lord has mercy, and they are the People of the Truth (ahl al-haqq), who do not differ. And His saying: ﴿and for that He created them﴾, concerning which there are several opinions:

The first: what is related from Mujahid, that he said: "And for mercy He created them." This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "And for disagreement He created them." This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, and from al-Hasan al-Basri in another narration: He created the people of Paradise for Paradise, and He created the people of the Fire for the Fire, and He created the people of misery for misery, and He created the people of happiness for happiness.

Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Salam said: "What I choose as the meaning of the verse is that He created one group for mercy and one group for punishment." He said: "And this is the position of the Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah)."

Some of them mentioned that the intended meaning of the verse is that the People of Falsehood (ahl al-batil) differ, while the People of Truth agree, and He created the People of Falsehood for disagreement and the People of Truth for agreement.

An-Nahhas said: "This is the clearest of the opinions and the most expansive."

Abu 'Ubayd argued for the meaning he claimed by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together"﴾. He said: its meaning is: "And the decree of your Lord has been fulfilled: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together."

It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said, relating from Allah the dispute between Paradise and the Fire: He said to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will of My servants." And He said to the Fire: "You are My punishment; I punish through you whomever I will." "And each of you has its fullness."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 120:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And all that We relate to you of the news of the messengers is that by which We make your heart firm﴾. Its meaning: all that you need of the news of the messengers, We relate it to you so that your heart may be made firm by it. If it is said: his heart was already firm, so what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿so that We may make your heart firm thereby﴾?

We say: its meaning is that you may increase in firmness. This is like His, the Exalted's, saying in the story of Abraham: ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿and in this there has come to you the truth﴾, most scholars hold that its meaning is: there has come to you in this surah the truth. And some of them said: there has come to you in this world (al-dunya) the truth.

If it is said: what is the benefit in specifying this surah, when the truth has come to him in every surah?

We say: its benefit is the honouring of the surah. Its being singled out for honour does not indicate that the truth did not come to him in other than it. Do you not see that a person says: "So-and-so is in the truth" when death attends him, though he was in the truth before it and after it?

His saying: ﴿and an admonition﴾ means: and there has come to you an admonition, ﴿and a reminder for the believers﴾, i.e., a reminding for the believers.

Al-Sam'ani's commentary on Surah 11, verse 121:

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And say to those who do not believe: "Work according to your standing; indeed we are working."﴾ The meaning of the verse is threat and warning, as we have explained before.

Verse 11:122 reads: ﴿And wait, indeed we are waiting.﴾

Wait, I need to check the instruction: the passage is "وَقَوله: ﴿وَانْتَظرُوا إِنَّا منتظرون﴾ فِي معنى الْآيَة." Translation:

And His saying: ﴿And wait, indeed we are waiting﴾ — concerning the meaning of the verse.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 11, verse 123:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: to Allah belongs the knowledge of what is hidden in the heavens and the earth.

And His saying: ﴿And to Him the whole matter will be returned, so worship Him and rely upon Him﴾. Its meaning: to Him the affair of the servants will be returned, and He will recompense them for good and evil. ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾, meaning: nothing of the deeds of the servants is hidden from Him, however small it may be. And Allah knows best.

Completed, by the praise of Allah, the second volume of the Tafsir of Abu al-Muzaffar al-Sam'ani, and it is followed by the third volume, God willing, which begins with the tafsir of Surah Yusuf.
